subtype: Approach: switching tactics after a bad practice score [Revision]
passage: Lavanya sat on the string cot outside her house in the village and made a quiz for herself, ten questions from her science chapter. She had read it twice. She scored five out of ten. She looked at the paper for a while. "Reading is not working," she said quietly. That evening her brother Ramesh saw her cutting a notebook page into small cards. On each she wrote a point on one side and a question on the other. She shuffled and tested herself. The next night she quizzed herself again and got eight right.

qa.q: What score did Lavanya get on her first quiz?
qa.a: She scored five out of ten.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel after looking at her score of five out of ten?
qa.a: She was disappointed but clear-headed. She quietly said reading was not working, which led her to change her method.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Lavanya add to her cards, and why?
qa.a: She could ask Ramesh to read her the questions. Answering out loud to someone else helps her practise saying it.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Lavanya cutting the notebook page into cards?
qa.a: Ramesh sees his sister trying something new after a poor score, and he may be curious or proud. He notices her working hard on her own.

grounding: After scoring five out of ten on her own quiz, a girl notices reading alone is not working and switches to key-point cards she uses to quiz herself, and her next score rises.

subtype: Approach: switching tactics after a bad practice score [Revision]
passage: Elif had read her history notes on the Romans four times, so she made herself a quiz: ten questions from the chapter, answered with the notes face down. She checked. Five out of ten. She stared at the red crosses on the bus home through north London. Reading and reading hadn't made it stick. That evening she cut an old cereal box into cards. On one side, a question: Why did the Romans build straight roads? On the other, the answer in her own words. She shuffled them and tested herself, putting wrong ones in a pile to redo. On Thursday she tried a new quiz. Nine out of ten. She texted Kofi: 'Cards work!! 🎉'

qa.q: What did Elif score on her first quiz?
What was Elif feeling as she stared at the red crosses on the bus?
qa.a: She seemed disappointed and frustrated, because reading the notes four times hadn't made them stick.

qa.q: What else could Elif do with her wrong-answer pile?
qa.a: Go through it again the next day until it's empty; the cards work because they make her recall, not just reread.

qa.q: How might Kofi see Elif's text?
qa.a: Kofi gets an excited message and may want to try cards too, especially after hearing about the jump to nine.

grounding: Shows a child noticing from a five-out-of-ten quiz that rereading isn't working, switching to question cards, and scoring higher next time.

subtype: Approach: switching tactics after a bad practice score [Revision]
passage: In the school library, Dilnaz marked her own practice quiz on the digestive system. Five out of ten. She had read the chapter three times that week. She sat back and chewed her pen. Reading isn't going in, she thought. It just slides past. She asked the librarian for some old index cards and wrote the key points: one part of the body on each card, its job on the back. For two days she flipped through them in every free period, putting the ones she missed at the bottom. On Friday Vaibhav, from her table, asked her ten questions from the book. She got eight. 'What changed?' he asked. She waved the stack of cards.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz's practice quiz about?
What was Dilnaz thinking and feeling when she chewed her pen?
qa.a: She was frustrated that the reading 'just slides past', and was working out that she needed a different way to study.

qa.q: What would keep Dilnaz's score rising?
qa.a: Keep testing herself with the cards, especially the ones she keeps missing; switching after the low score is what made the difference.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see the change?
qa.a: Vaibhav notices the jump to eight and is curious enough to ask what changed.

grounding: Illustrates a child who scores five out of ten, sees reading alone isn't working, switches to self-quizzing with cards, and improves.
